newsitem.title: USA: NYS approves transit agency's budget - reports.
newsitem.headline: NYS approves transit agency's budget - reports.

text.p: New York State lawmakers finally approved an $11.9 billion capital budget for the state transit agency on Thursday evening, enabling it to go ahead with plans to buy new subway cars, newspapers said on Friday.

The New York Times said the Metropolitan Transportation Authority's new spending plan provides $7.3 billion for new buses, subway and commuter trains and station renovations from the start of this year to the end of 1999. The $11.9 billion total includes 1995 and 1996 projects.
The Daily News said that the Transit Authority will get about $9.08 billion, while commuter railroads will split the remaining $2.9 billion.

Had the pact not been approved last night, the Metropolitan Transportation Authority could have had to renegotiate contracts for over 1,000 new subway cars with Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Bombardier Inc. The Times said the two suppliers extended a June 30 deadline until Friday.

However, the paper said that the state transit agency will have to rely much more heavily than in the past on borrowed money, $3.5 billion that riders' fares will have to repay. That is because the $96 million of state aid is a big drop from past capital programs.

The transit agency will be allowed to use part of a transit reserve fund, a pool fed by taxes in the downstate region on items like petroleum products. The $15 million a year will be used to pay for service cuts made in 1995, the paper said.
The Daily News added the capital spending plan includes $704 million for 235 buses.
And Metropolitan Transportation Authority will pay $30 million for a $315 million conversion of the Manhattan's central post office into an Amtrak station.

The New York Times said the new plan for the post office was scaled down from a bigger project, which was estimated to cost over $435 million, and which included a 120-foot-high skylight over the post office as well as retail improvements at the existing station.

The smaller project that was approved will be paid for as follows: $100 million of federal aid, $75 million from the state, $25 million from the city and $115 million from private business through the development of retail space in the new station.
